exhibits.title: Antikythera mechanism
exhibits.hook: Bronze gears that modelled the heavens, recovered from a two-thousand-year-old shipwreck.
exhibits.caption: Recovered from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, this geared bronze device computed astronomical positions and eclipses. Its complexity was not matched for more than a thousand years. It is the earliest known analog computer.
exhibits.caveat: The label 'earliest known analog computer' reflects surviving evidence; earlier geared devices may not have survived.
exhibits.narration: Recovered from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, this geared bronze device computed astronomical positions and eclipses. Its complexity was not matched for more than a thousand years. It is the earliest known analog computer.

exhibits.title: Al-Khwarizmi and the word "algorithm"
exhibits.hook: One scholar, two words: his name became algorithm, his book became algebra.
exhibits.caption: The mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote the book that named algebra, and his own name, Latinized as Algoritmi, became the word algorithm. His step-by-step methods for arithmetic and equation solving are the ancestors of every program.
exhibits.narration: The mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote the book that named algebra, and his own name, written in Latin as Algoritmi, became the word algorithm. His step by step methods for arithmetic and equation solving are the ancestors of every program.

exhibits.title: Jacquard's punched-card loom
exhibits.hook: Punched cards ran a loom two centuries before they ran a computer.
exhibits.caption: Joseph Marie Jacquard's loom wove patterns from a chain of punched cards, so one machine could produce many designs without being rebuilt. The idea of a punched-card program later inspired Babbage and Hollerith.
exhibits.narration: Joseph Marie Jacquard's loom wove patterns from a chain of punched cards, so one machine could produce many designs without being rebuilt. The idea of a punched card program later inspired Babbage and Hollerith.

exhibits.title: Babbage's Difference & Analytical Engines
exhibits.hook: Two engines, one idea: a computer that runs on numbers and never tires.
exhibits.caption: Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine to compute mathematical tables, and the Analytical Engine to run any calculation from punched cards. Neither was finished in his lifetime, but the Analytical Engine's design held every part of a modern computer: a store, a mill, and control by a program.
exhibits.narration: Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine to compute mathematical tables, and the Analytical Engine to run any calculation from punched cards. Neither engine was finished in his lifetime, but the Analytical Engine's design held every part of a modern computer: a store, a mill, and control by a program.

exhibits.title: Ada Lovelace's Note G
exhibits.hook: The first published algorithm, written for a machine that was never built.
exhibits.caption: Ada Lovelace's 1843 notes on the Analytical Engine include Note G, which steps through a method for computing Bernoulli numbers. It is widely read as the first published algorithm written for a computing machine.
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' applies to the published algorithm in Note G, not to a working machine.
exhibits.narration: Ada Lovelace's notes from 1843 on the Analytical Engine include Note G, which steps through a method for computing Bernoulli numbers. It is widely read as the first published algorithm written for a computing machine.

exhibits.title: Boole's algebra of logic
exhibits.hook: True or false: the two-state logic inside every computer was written down in 1854.
exhibits.caption: George Boole's 1854 book reduced logic to algebra, with variables that are only ever true or false. A century later his rules became the foundation of digital circuit design.
exhibits.narration: George Boole's book from 1854 reduced logic to algebra, with variables that are only ever true or false. A century later, his rules became the foundation of digital circuit design.

exhibits.title: Hollerith's census tabulator
exhibits.hook: Punched cards counted a nation, and a census job launched IBM.
exhibits.caption: Herman Hollerith's punched-card tabulator counted the 1890 United States census far faster than hand tallying. His Tabulating Machine Company later grew into IBM.
exhibits.narration: Herman Hollerith's punched card tabulator counted the 1890 United States census far faster than hand tallying. His Tabulating Machine Company later grew into IBM.

exhibits.title: Turing's universal machine
exhibits.caption: Alan Turing, 1936: a tape, a head and a table of rules can carry out any computation. This machine adds 1 to a binary number. Step it and watch the carry ripple left.
exhibits.narration: In 1936, Alan Turing described a machine with a tape, a read and write head, and a small table of rules. He showed that it could carry out any computation that a person could follow step by step. This exhibit adds one to a binary number. Step it, and watch the carry ripple to the left.

exhibits.title: Shannon: circuits as Boolean logic
exhibits.hook: One thesis joined algebra to electricity, and every logic gate descends from it.
exhibits.caption: Claude Shannon's 1937 master's thesis showed that electrical switches could carry out Boolean logic. It linked algebra and circuits and is often called the most important master's thesis of the century.

exhibits.title: Bletchley Park: Bombe & Colossus
exhibits.hook: Codebreaking machines that helped shorten a war and pioneered the programmable computer.
exhibits.caption: At Bletchley Park, the Bombe helped break German Enigma messages, and in 1944 Colossus attacked the Lorenz cipher. Colossus used valves and paper tape and is counted as the first programmable electronic digital computer.
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' applies to Colossus as a programmable electronic digital computer.
exhibits.narration: At Bletchley Park, the Bombe helped break German Enigma messages, and in 1944 Colossus attacked the Lorenz cipher. Colossus used valves and paper tape, and it is counted as the first programmable electronic digital computer.

exhibits.title: Information theory
exhibits.hook: One paper, one bit: how to measure information itself.
exhibits.caption: Claude Shannon's 1948 paper, A Mathematical Theory of Communication, defined the bit and showed how much information a channel can carry. It founded information theory and underpins every digital system built since.

sources.label: Wikipedia: A Mathematical Theory of Communication

exhibits.narration: Claude Shannon's 1948 paper, A Mathematical Theory of Communication, defined the bit and showed how much information a channel can carry. It founded information theory and underpins every digital system built since.

exhibits.title: Dijkstra's shortest path
exhibits.hook: Three pages in 1959 that still route your car and your packets.
exhibits.caption: Edsger Dijkstra's 1959 algorithm finds the shortest route through a graph without needing a map of the whole network. It still steers car navigation and internet routing today.

stats.v: A Note on Two Problems in Connexion with Graphs

exhibits.narration: Edsger Dijkstra's algorithm from 1959 finds the shortest route through a graph without needing a map of the whole network. It still steers car navigation and internet routing today.

exhibits.title: NP-completeness
exhibits.hook: A million hard problems, one shared difficulty, and a question still open.
exhibits.caption: Stephen Cook's 1971 theorem showed that many hard problems are all equally hard: solve one fast and you solve them all. The P versus NP question it opened remains unsolved.
exhibits.narration: Stephen Cook's theorem from 1971 showed that many hard problems are all equally hard: solve one fast and you solve them all. The P versus NP question it opened remains unsolved.

exhibits.title: Public-key crypto: Diffie-Hellman, RSA
exhibits.hook: Two keys, one public and one secret: encryption without a shared secret.
exhibits.caption: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman proposed public-key cryptography in 1976, so two people could agree on a secret over a public channel. In 1977 Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman turned the idea into RSA.
exhibits.narration: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman proposed public key cryptography in 1976, so two people could agree on a secret over a public channel. In 1977, Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman turned the idea into RSA.

exhibits.title: Shor's algorithm
exhibits.hook: A quantum factoring trick that put every RSA key on notice.
exhibits.caption: Peter Shor's 1994 algorithm showed a quantum computer could factor large numbers fast, which would break RSA encryption. It made quantum computing a matter of real urgency.

stats.v: exponentially faster than known classical methods

exhibits.narration: Peter Shor's algorithm from 1994 showed that a quantum computer could factor large numbers fast, which would break RSA encryption. It made quantum computing a matter of real urgency.

exhibits.title: Post-quantum crypto standards
exhibits.hook: New math, new standards, written before the quantum computer that would break the old ones.
exhibits.caption: In 2024 NIST published the first standardized post-quantum algorithms, designed to resist attack by a quantum computer. They replace today’s key exchange and signatures before a large quantum machine arrives.
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first standardized post-quantum algorithms' refers to NIST's finalized standards.
exhibits.narration: In 2024, NIST published the first standardized post quantum algorithms, designed to resist attack by a quantum computer. They replace today’s key exchange and signatures before a large quantum machine arrives.

exhibits.title: Zuse Z3
exhibits.hook: Relays and punched film, running programs in Berlin in 1941.
exhibits.caption: Konrad Zuse's Z3, completed in Berlin in 1941, was the first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer. It ran on relays and was controlled by punched film.
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' refers to a working programmable, fully automatic digital computer; earlier machines were not both programmable and automatic.
exhibits.narration: Konrad Zuse's Z3, completed in Berlin in 1941, was the first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer. It ran on relays and was controlled by punched film.

exhibits.title: ENIAC
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' applies to general-purpose electronic digital computers, not to computing machines as a whole.
exhibits.caption: The first general-purpose electronic digital computer, completed in 1945 and unveiled in February 1946. Every glowing dot in this portal stands for 50 of its vacuum tubes. Some just burned out: find them and swap them.
exhibits.narration: ENIAC was the first general-purpose electronic digital computer. It was finished in 1945 and unveiled in February 1946. Inside sat about seventeen thousand five hundred vacuum tubes, and the machine weighed about twenty-seven tons. It could run five thousand additions every second. In this portal, every glowing dot stands for fifty tubes. Some have just burned out. Find them and swap them.

exhibits.title: The transistor
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' refers to the transistor of 1947 and the silicon transistor of 1954.
exhibits.caption: Bell Labs built the first transistor in 1947 from germanium, and Morris Tanenbaum made the first silicon one there in 1954. A switch with no filament to burn out. Flip the base and watch current flow.
exhibits.narration: Bell Labs built the first transistor in 1947, from germanium. In 1954, Morris Tanenbaum made the first silicon one there. The work won the Nobel Prize in 1956. A transistor is a switch with no filament to burn out. Flip the base in this portal and watch the current flow.

exhibits.title: Manchester Baby: first stored program
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' refers to running a stored program, not to being the first computer.
exhibits.hook: The first machine to run a program stored in its own memory.
exhibits.caption: On June 21, 1948, the Manchester Baby ran the first program stored in electronic memory. The program lived in the same store as the data, the pattern every computer since has followed.
exhibits.narration: On June 21, 1948, the Manchester Baby ran the first program stored in electronic memory. The program lived in the same store as the data, the pattern every computer since has followed.

exhibits.title: The integrated circuit
exhibits.hook: A whole circuit, shrunk onto a single piece of silicon.
exhibits.caption: Jack Kilby built the first integrated circuit in 1958, and Robert Noyce made a silicon version in 1959 that was easier to mass produce. Putting many components on one chip made the microelectronics revolution possible.

sources.label: Computer History Museum: The Silicon Engine

exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' refers to Kilby's 1958 demonstration and Noyce's 1959 silicon version.
exhibits.narration: Jack Kilby built the first integrated circuit in 1958, and Robert Noyce made a silicon version in 1959 that was easier to mass produce. Putting many components on one chip made the microelectronics revolution possible.

exhibits.title: Moore's law
exhibits.hook: A prediction that became a deadline.
exhibits.caption: In 1965 Gordon Moore predicted that the number of components on a chip would double roughly every year, a pace later revised to every two years. The industry has treated his observation as a roadmap ever since.

stats.v: doubling every one to two years
an observation, not a physical law

exhibits.narration: In 1965, Gordon Moore predicted that the number of components on a chip would double roughly every year, a pace later revised to every two years. The industry has treated his observation as a roadmap ever since.

exhibits.title: Intel 4004 microprocessor
exhibits.hook: A whole CPU on one chip, first sold for calculators.
exhibits.caption: The Intel 4004, released in 1971, packed a 4-bit central processing unit onto a single chip. It was the first commercially available microprocessor, putting a computer brain in a package the size of a fingernail.
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' refers to a commercially available single-chip microprocessor.
exhibits.narration: The Intel 4004, released in 1971, packed a four bit central processing unit onto a single chip. It was the first commercially available microprocessor, putting a computer brain in a package the size of a fingernail.

exhibits.title: Cray-1 supercomputer
exhibits.hook: A machine shaped like a C, built to keep its wires as short as possible.
exhibits.caption: Seymour Cray's Cray-1, shipped in 1976, was shaped like a C to shorten its wiring and defined the supercomputer race of the 1970s and 1980s. It made vector computing famous.
exhibits.caveat: Performance claims reflect the Cray-1 at its 1976 introduction, relative to machines of its time.
exhibits.narration: Seymour Cray's Cray-1, shipped in 1976, was shaped like a C to shorten its wiring, and it defined the supercomputer race of the 1970s and 1980s. It made vector computing famous.

exhibits.title: ARM1
exhibits.hook: A chip made by a small team in 1985, now inside nearly every phone.
exhibits.caption: The ARM1, finished at Acorn in 1985, was a deliberately simple RISC chip designed by a small team. Its low-power design now runs inside billions of phones and embedded devices.
exhibits.narration: The ARM1, finished at Acorn in 1985, was a deliberately simple RISC chip designed by a small team. Its low power design now runs inside billions of phones and embedded devices.

exhibits.title: CUDA & GPU computing
exhibits.hook: The graphics card learns to do general computing.
exhibits.caption: Nvidia released CUDA in 2007, opening the graphics processing unit to general-purpose computing. Thousands of small cores running together made GPUs the engine of the deep learning boom.
exhibits.narration: Nvidia released CUDA in 2007, opening the graphics processing unit to general purpose computing. Thousands of small cores running together made GPUs the engine of the deep learning boom.

exhibits.title: Tensor Processing Unit
exhibits.caption: AI accelerators are built around matrix multiply. A systolic array pulses data through a grid of multiply-accumulate cells, so every value is reused without another trip to memory.
exhibits.narration: AI accelerators are built around matrix multiply. A systolic array pulses data through a grid of multiply and accumulate cells, so every value is reused without another trip to memory. The first TPU went into service in 2015, and its matrix unit was two hundred fifty-six by two hundred fifty-six.

exhibits.title: Quantum processors
exhibits.hook: Qubits in, one contested milestone out.
exhibits.caption: Quantum processors like Google's Sycamore, announced in 2019, run on qubits instead of bits. Their claimed advantage on one sampling task is still debated.
exhibits.caveat: Quantum advantage claims for the 2019 Sycamore experiment are contested and refer to one specific sampling task.
exhibits.narration: Quantum processors like Google's Sycamore, announced in 2019, run on qubits instead of bits. Their claimed advantage on one sampling task is still debated.

exhibits.title: Patch-cable programming
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' refers to the programmers who set up ENIAC by rewiring its cables and switches.
exhibits.caption: ENIAC’s first programmers, including Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings and Frances Bilas, set up each problem by rewiring cables and switches. Changing the program meant changing the machine.
exhibits.narration: ENIAC's first programmers, including Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings and Frances Bilas, set up each problem by rewiring cables and switches. Changing the program meant changing the machine itself. The program was the wiring. The idea of a stored program, one that lives in memory instead of in cables, came with EDVAC in 1945.

exhibits.title: Hopper's A-0 compiler
exhibits.hook: Grace Hopper's first step from machine code to words.
exhibits.caption: Grace Hopper's A-0 system, finished in 1952, translated symbolic instructions into machine code for the UNIVAC I. It was an early compiler, a first step toward programming in something closer to English.
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' applies to the A-0 system as an early compiler, not to a compiler in today's full sense.
exhibits.narration: Grace Hopper's A-0 system, finished in 1952, translated symbolic instructions into machine code for the UNIVAC I. It was an early compiler, a first step toward programming in something closer to English.

exhibits.title: FORTRAN & LISP
exhibits.caption: FORTRAN let engineers write formulas instead of machine code; IBM shipped its compiler in 1957. One line of code was one 80-column card, and a program was a deck. Pick a statement and punch it.
exhibits.narration: FORTRAN let engineers write formulas instead of machine code. IBM shipped its compiler in 1957. One line of code was one card, eighty columns wide, and a program was a deck of cards. Its sibling LISP arrived at MIT in 1958. Pick a statement in this portal and punch it.

exhibits.title: COBOL
exhibits.hook: English-like code from 1959, still settling your bank's books.
exhibits.caption: COBOL, specified in 1959 by a committee that included Grace Hopper, was written to read like English so business people could understand it. Decades later it still runs much of banking and government.
exhibits.narration: COBOL, specified in 1959 by a committee that included Grace Hopper, was written to read like English so business people could understand it. Decades later, it still runs much of banking and government.

exhibits.title: Software engineering & Apollo code
exhibits.hook: A conference coined the field, and Apollo flew its code to the Moon.
exhibits.caption: The term software engineering was coined at a 1968 NATO conference as projects grew too big to hand-craft. The next year Margaret Hamilton's team flew the Apollo 11 guidance software to the Moon.
exhibits.narration: The term software engineering was coined at a 1968 NATO conference as projects grew too big to hand craft. The next year, Margaret Hamilton's team flew the Apollo 11 guidance software to the Moon.

exhibits.title: Unix & C
exhibits.hook: An operating system and a language that still run the world.
exhibits.caption: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie built Unix at Bell Labs in 1969, and Ritchie designed C in 1972 to rewrite it. Unix tools and the portability of C became the foundation of modern software.
exhibits.narration: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie built Unix at Bell Labs in 1969, and Ritchie designed C in 1972 to rewrite it. Unix tools and the portability of C became the foundation of modern software.

exhibits.title: Relational databases
exhibits.hook: Data as tables, and a language to ask them questions.
exhibits.caption: Edgar Codd's 1970 paper described data as relations, or tables, that could be queried in a uniform way. The relational model became the basis of SQL and nearly every database in use today.
exhibits.narration: Edgar Codd's 1970 paper described data as relations, or tables, that could be queried in a uniform way. The relational model became the basis of SQL and nearly every database in use today.

exhibits.title: GNU & Linux
exhibits.hook: A free operating system, built in public by thousands.
exhibits.caption: Richard Stallman launched the GNU project in 1983 to build a free operating system, and Linus Torvalds released the Linux kernel in 1991. Together they power most of the servers on the internet and every Android phone.
exhibits.narration: Richard Stallman launched the GNU project in 1983 to build a free operating system, and Linus Torvalds released the Linux kernel in 1991. Together they power most of the servers on the internet and every Android phone.

exhibits.title: Git
exhibits.hook: Built in a hurry for one kernel, now holding up most of the internet.
exhibits.caption: Linus Torvalds wrote Git in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel after its previous tool became unavailable. Its distributed, branch-friendly design now underpins most of the world's software.
exhibits.narration: Linus Torvalds wrote Git in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel after its previous tool became unavailable. Its distributed, branch friendly design now underpins most of the world's software.

exhibits.title: Bundle Tower: React & Next.js
exhibits.caption: React, Next.js and the Python data stack made software composable, and pages heavier. Each square in this portal is one kilobyte.
exhibits.narration: React, Next.js and the modern web stack made software composable, and made pages heavier. In this portal, each square stands for one kilobyte. The median mobile page of 2025 is about two point five six megabytes, with seventy-five requests and over six hundred kilobytes of JavaScript.

exhibits.title: ARPANET
exhibits.hook: The first packet-switched network, with a first message that crashed.
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' refers to the first ARPANET message, sent on October 29, 1969.
exhibits.caption: ARPANET went live in 1969, connecting four university sites by packet switching. Its first message, LOGIN from UCLA to Stanford, crashed after two letters, but the network grew into the internet.
exhibits.narration: ARPANET went live in 1969, connecting four university sites by packet switching. Its first message, LOGIN from UCLA to Stanford, crashed after two letters, but the network grew into the internet.

exhibits.title: Email
exhibits.hook: One message, one symbol: the @ that joined a person to a machine.
exhibits.caption: In 1971 Ray Tomlinson sent the first message between computers over the ARPANET and chose the @ sign to join a user to a machine. His choice of separator became universal.
exhibits.caveat: The 'first' claim refers to networked email between machines; earlier single-system mailbox programs existed.
exhibits.narration: In 1971, Ray Tomlinson sent the first message between computers over the ARPANET, and he chose the at sign to join a user to a machine. His choice of separator became universal.

exhibits.title: Ethernet
exhibits.hook: One sketch on one shared wire, wired into every office since.
exhibits.caption: Robert Metcalfe sketched Ethernet at Xerox PARC in 1973 as a shared wire for office computers. It became the standard way to wire local networks.
exhibits.narration: Robert Metcalfe sketched Ethernet at Xerox PARC in 1973 as a shared wire for office computers. It became the standard way to wire local networks.

exhibits.title: TCP/IP
exhibits.hook: The common language that let different networks speak.
exhibits.caption: Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn described TCP in 1974 as a way to connect separate networks into an internet. On January 1, 1983, ARPANET switched to TCP/IP, the event many mark as the internet's birthday.
exhibits.narration: Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn described TCP in 1974 as a way to connect separate networks into an internet. On January 1, 1983, ARPANET switched to TCP and IP, the event many mark as the internet's birthday.

exhibits.title: DNS
exhibits.hook: The phone book of the internet, replacing one file that everyone edited.
exhibits.caption: Paul Mockapetris designed the Domain Name System in 1983 to replace a single hand-edited hosts file. It turned names like example.com into addresses across a distributed network.
exhibits.narration: Paul Mockapetris designed the Domain Name System in 1983 to replace a single hand edited hosts file. It turned names like example dot com into addresses across a distributed network.

exhibits.title: NeXT + dial-up
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' describes the common early dial-up experience, not a claim that a single machine was the web's only origin.
exhibits.caption: The web was written on a NeXT computer at CERN, and most people first reached it through a dial-up modem. Race the first web page against a 2025 median home page over a 14.4 kbit/s line.
exhibits.narration: The web was written on a NeXT computer at CERN, and most people first reached it through a dial-up modem. Over a fourteen point four kilobit line, the first page was tiny. Race that first page against a 2025 median page and feel the difference.

exhibits.title: HTML & HTTP
exhibits.caption: About 18 elements and one method, GET. Flip the article into 1991 mode: the styling, scripts and images vanish, and the meaning stays.
exhibits.narration: The first web had about eighteen HTML elements and one HTTP method: GET. Flip the article into 1991 mode in this portal. The styling, the scripts and the images vanish, and the meaning stays. CSS would not arrive until 1996.

exhibits.title: Mosaic browser
exhibits.hook: The browser that put pictures on pages and the web on the map.
exhibits.caption: NCSA Mosaic, released in 1993, put images and text on the same web page and became the first browser used by the millions. It is widely credited with igniting the web boom.
exhibits.caveat: The 'first browser used by the millions' claim reflects popularity, not the first graphical browser; earlier graphical browsers existed.
exhibits.narration: NCSA Mosaic, released in 1993, put images and text on the same web page, and it became the first browser used by the millions. It is widely credited with igniting the web boom.

exhibits.title: Search: PageRank
exhibits.hook: Rank pages by who links to them, and the web reorganizes itself.
exhibits.caption: Larry Page and Sergey Brin's 1998 PageRank ranked web pages by counting their incoming links. It powered Google's search and changed how the web is organized.
exhibits.narration: Larry Page and Sergey Brin's PageRank, published in 1998, ranked web pages by counting their incoming links. It powered Google's search and changed how the web is organized.

exhibits.title: Wikipedia
exhibits.hook: An encyclopedia with no entry fee and millions of editors.
exhibits.caption: Wikipedia launched in 2001 as a free encyclopedia anyone could edit. It became one of the world's most read websites, written and checked by volunteers.
exhibits.narration: Wikipedia launched in 2001 as a free encyclopedia anyone could edit. It became one of the world's most read websites, written and checked by volunteers.

exhibits.title: The cloud: AWS
exhibits.hook: Computing on demand, billed like a utility.
exhibits.caption: Amazon Web Services launched S3 storage and EC2 compute in 2006, letting anyone rent servers by the hour over the internet. The cloud turned computing into a utility and became the default way software runs.
exhibits.narration: Amazon Web Services launched S3 storage and EC2 compute in 2006, letting anyone rent servers by the hour over the internet. The cloud turned computing into a utility and became the default way software runs.

exhibits.title: Spacewar!
exhibits.hook: Two ships, one star, and a game written on a minicomputer in 1962.
exhibits.caption: In 1962 Steve Russell and friends at MIT built Spacewar! on a PDP-1 minicomputer. The two-player space duel is one of the earliest video games and the direct ancestor of the arcade.
exhibits.caveat: The 'one of the earliest' claim reflects surviving evidence; earlier experiments like OXO and Tennis for Two exist.
exhibits.narration: In 1962, Steve Russell and friends at MIT built Spacewar on a PDP-1 minicomputer. The two player space duel is one of the earliest video games and the direct ancestor of the arcade.

exhibits.title: Sketchpad
exhibits.hook: Draw with a light pen, and the computer understands.
exhibits.caption: Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad, from his 1963 MIT thesis, let a user draw on screen with a light pen and move shapes as objects. It pioneered interactive computer graphics and the idea of the graphical interface.
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' applies to Sketchpad as the first interactive computer graphics program.
exhibits.narration: Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad, from his 1963 MIT thesis, let a user draw on screen with a light pen and move shapes as objects. It pioneered interactive computer graphics and the idea of the graphical interface.

exhibits.title: Engelbart's demo
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' applies to the December 9, 1968 demonstration as the first public showing of the mouse and of these capabilities together. The mouse itself was a 1964 prototype built by Bill English, and earlier pointing devices existed.
exhibits.hook: The mouse, the window, the link and live shared editing, all on one 1968 stage.
exhibits.caption: On December 9, 1968, Douglas Engelbart showed the mouse, windows, hypertext links and live shared editing in one ninety-minute demo in San Francisco. Many parts of how you use a computer today appeared on that stage. Move the pointer and click a link to jump between notes while a second cursor types beside you.
exhibits.narration: On December ninth, nineteen sixty-eight, Douglas Engelbart showed the mouse, windows, hypertext links and live shared editing in one ninety minute demo in San Francisco. Many parts of how you use a computer today appeared on that stage. Move the pointer and click a link to jump between notes, while a second cursor types beside you.

sources.label: Computer History Museum, Prototype Engelbart Mouse

exhibits.title: Xerox Alto
exhibits.hook: Windows, a mouse and a screen full of pixels, all in 1973.
exhibits.caption: The Xerox Alto, built in 1973, was the first computer designed around a graphical interface with windows, a mouse and a bitmap screen. It inspired the Macintosh and nearly every computer since.
exhibits.caveat: The 'first' claim refers to a computer designed around the graphical interface; earlier research systems like the NLS preceded it.
exhibits.narration: The Xerox Alto, built in 1973, was the first computer designed around a graphical interface with windows, a mouse and a bitmap screen. It inspired the Macintosh and nearly every computer since.

exhibits.title: Altair 8800 & Apple II
exhibits.hook: From blinking-front-panel hobby kit to a computer for the home.
exhibits.caption: The Altair 8800, sold in 1975, popularized the microcomputer among hobbyists. The Apple II, shipped in 1977, made computing a home product with colour graphics and a built-in BASIC.
exhibits.narration: The Altair 8800, sold in 1975, popularized the microcomputer among hobbyists. The Apple II, shipped in 1977, made computing a home product with colour graphics and a built in BASIC.

exhibits.title: IBM PC & Macintosh
exhibits.hook: The business machine, then the machine everyone could point and click.
exhibits.caption: The IBM PC, released in 1981, set the standard for personal computers in business. In 1984 the Macintosh brought the mouse and a graphical interface to a mass audience.
exhibits.caveat: The label 'first' applies to the Macintosh as a successful mass-market computer with a graphical interface, not the first machine to have one.
exhibits.narration: The IBM PC, released in 1981, set the standard for personal computers in business. In 1984, the Macintosh brought the mouse and a graphical interface to a mass audience.

exhibits.title: Smartphone & multi-touch
exhibits.hook: A computer in your pocket, operated by touch.
exhibits.caption: The iPhone, announced in 2007, combined a phone, an internet device and a music player behind a multi-touch screen. Direct manipulation by touch changed how billions of people use computers.
exhibits.narration: The iPhone, announced in 2007, combined a phone, an internet device and a music player behind a multi touch screen. Direct manipulation by touch changed how billions of people use computers.

exhibits.title: Screen readers go mainstream
exhibits.hook: A computer that reads its own screen aloud, now built into the phone.
exhibits.caption: By 2009 screen readers had moved from specialist software into mainstream devices, led by VoiceOver on the iPhone 3GS. They read interfaces aloud so blind and low-vision people can use them.

stats.v: access for blind and low-vision users

exhibits.narration: By 2009, screen readers had moved from specialist software into mainstream devices, led by VoiceOver on the iPhone 3GS. They read interfaces aloud so blind and low vision people can use them.

exhibits.title: The Turing test
exhibits.hook: Can a machine pass for human? The question was posed in 1950.
exhibits.caption: Alan Turing's 1950 paper proposed the Imitation Game: if a machine's replies are indistinguishable from a person's, call it intelligent. The test still frames debates about machine intelligence.
exhibits.narration: Alan Turing's paper from 1950 proposed the Imitation Game: if a machine's replies are indistinguishable from a person's, call it intelligent. The test still frames debates about machine intelligence.

exhibits.title: Dartmouth Workshop
exhibits.caption: Summer 1956: the workshop whose 1955 proposal coined “artificial intelligence.” Meet the four proposers, then run the Logic Theorist on Principia Mathematica.
exhibits.narration: In the summer of 1956, a small workshop at Dartmouth College gathered the people who would name the field. The 1955 proposal that set it up coined the term artificial intelligence. Meet the four proposers, then run the Logic Theorist on Principia Mathematica, where it proved thirty-eight of fifty-two theorems.

exhibits.title: The Perceptron
exhibits.hook: A machine that could learn, one adjustable weight at a time.
exhibits.caption: Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron, demonstrated in 1958, was an early artificial neuron that learned by adjusting its weights. It could recognise simple patterns, and its limits later motivated the work that powers neural networks today.
exhibits.narration: Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron, demonstrated in 1958, was an early artificial neuron that learned by adjusting its weights. It could recognise simple patterns, and its limits later motivated the work that powers neural networks today.

exhibits.title: ELIZA
exhibits.hook: A chatbot from 1966 that people opened up to, though it understood nothing.
exhibits.caption: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA, written in 1966, played a therapist by pattern-matching a user's words. People confided in it even though it understood nothing, the first hint of how persuasive chatbots can be.
exhibits.caveat: The 'first hint' phrasing is the author's framing of ELIZA's reception, not a measured historical first.
exhibits.narration: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA, written in 1966, played a therapist by pattern matching a user's words. People confided in it even though it understood nothing, the first hint of how persuasive chatbots can be.

exhibits.title: AI winters & expert systems
exhibits.hook: Twice the money dried up when the promises ran ahead of the machines.
exhibits.caption: Funding for artificial intelligence collapsed twice, in the mid 1970s and again around 1990, after grand promises failed to arrive. These AI winters followed hype cycles that the field still learns from.
exhibits.narration: Funding for artificial intelligence collapsed twice, in the mid 1970s and again around 1990, after grand promises failed to arrive. These AI winters followed hype cycles that the field still learns from.

exhibits.title: Backpropagation
exhibits.hook: Send the error backward, and the network teaches itself.
exhibits.caption: The 1986 paper by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularized backpropagation, the method that teaches a neural network by sending errors backward through it. It became the engine of modern deep learning.
exhibits.narration: The 1986 paper by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularized backpropagation, the method that teaches a neural network by sending errors backward through it. It became the engine of modern deep learning.

exhibits.title: Deep Blue
exhibits.caption: ChipTest (1985) and Deep Thought (1988) grew into IBM’s Deep Blue, which beat Garry Kasparov in 1997. Their strength was raw search. Drag the depth and watch the game tree explode.
exhibits.narration: IBM's chess machines grew from ChipTest in 1985 to Deep Thought in 1988, and then to Deep Blue, which beat Garry Kasparov in 1997. Their strength was raw search, looking at millions of positions every second. Drag the depth in this portal and watch the game tree explode.

exhibits.title: AlexNet & ImageNet
exhibits.hook: The moment deep learning went from lab curiosity to the main event.
exhibits.caption: AlexNet won the 2012 ImageNet competition by a wide margin, using a deep convolutional network trained on GPUs. Its victory launched the deep learning era that produced modern AI systems.
exhibits.narration: AlexNet won the 2012 ImageNet competition by a wide margin, using a deep convolutional network trained on GPUs. Its victory launched the deep learning era that produced modern AI systems.

exhibits.title: AlphaGo
exhibits.hook: Four games to one, in a game once thought beyond machines.
exhibits.caption: In March 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo beat the champion Lee Sedol four games to one. Its self-play and neural networks marked a leap for AI at a game once thought decades away.
exhibits.narration: In March 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo beat the champion Lee Sedol four games to one. Its self play and neural networks marked a leap for AI at a game once thought decades away.

exhibits.title: The Transformer
exhibits.caption: “Attention Is All You Need” (2017) introduced the Transformer, the architecture behind today’s Large Language Models. Every token decides how much to look at every other token. Click a word to see where it looks.
exhibits.narration: A 2017 paper called Attention Is All You Need introduced the Transformer, the architecture behind today's large language models. Its core idea is self-attention. Every token decides how much to look at every other token. Click a word in this portal to see where it looks.

exhibits.title: ChatGPT
exhibits.hook: The chatbot that made language models mainstream.
exhibits.caption: OpenAI released ChatGPT on November 30, 2022, a chatbot built on a large language model. It reached about a hundred million users in two months and made generative AI a daily tool.

stats.v: about 100 million users in two months

exhibits.caveat: Growth figures are estimates; user numbers changed quickly after launch.
exhibits.narration: OpenAI released ChatGPT on November 30, 2022, a chatbot built on a large language model. It reached about a hundred million users in two months and made generative AI a daily tool.

exhibits.title: The ENIAC Six
exhibits.hook: The women who programmed ENIAC by rewiring its cables.
exhibits.caption: Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas and Ruth Lichterman programmed the ENIAC by setting its cables and switches. They worked out the machine logic largely from block diagrams, and their story is now a landmark in the history of programming.
exhibits.narration: Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas and Ruth Lichterman programmed the ENIAC by setting its cables and switches. They worked out the machine logic largely from block diagrams, and their story is now a landmark in the history of programming.

exhibits.title: NASA's human computers
exhibits.hook: The people who did the math that put astronauts in orbit.
exhibits.caption: Before electronic machines, NASA's human computers, many of them Black women, calculated flight and orbital trajectories by hand. Katherine Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson became the best known of them.
exhibits.narration: Before electronic machines, NASA's human computers, many of them Black women, calculated flight and orbital trajectories by hand. Katherine Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson became the best known of them.

exhibits.title: Wall of names
exhibits.hook: A museum wall for the hands the plaques never named.
exhibits.caption: The wall of names honours the many contributors to computing whose work went uncredited, from operators and programmers to testers and educators. It is a reminder that every landmark was built by more hands than its plaque can hold.
exhibits.narration: The wall of names honours the many contributors to computing whose work went uncredited, from operators and programmers to testers and educators. It is a reminder that every landmark was built by more hands than its plaque can hold.

exhibits.title: Y2K
exhibits.hook: Two missing digits, and a worldwide scramble to add them back.
exhibits.caption: As the year 2000 approached, programs that stored years with two digits threatened to read 2000 as 1900. A worldwide remediation effort, estimated in the hundreds of billions of dollars, fixed most problems before they happened.
exhibits.narration: As the year 2000 approached, programs that stored years with two digits threatened to read 2000 as 1900. A worldwide remediation effort, estimated in the hundreds of billions of dollars, fixed most problems before they happened.

exhibits.title: GDPR & privacy
exhibits.hook: A law that put people, not companies, in charge of their data.
exhibits.caption: The EU's General Data Protection Regulation took effect in May 2018, giving people rights over their personal data. It became a global benchmark for privacy law and can levy fines of up to four percent of global turnover.
exhibits.narration: The EU's General Data Protection Regulation took effect in May 2018, giving people rights over their personal data. It became a global benchmark for privacy law and can levy fines of up to four percent of global turnover.

exhibits.title: The Bloat Audit
exhibits.hook: How heavy is the web? This museum measures its own weight.
exhibits.caption: The Bloat Audit turns the museum performance budget into an exhibit. It tracks the median web page, which grew to about 2.56 megabytes in 2025, and asks how much of that weight actually serves the visitor.
exhibits.narration: The Bloat Audit turns the museum performance budget into an exhibit. It tracks the median web page, which grew to about two point five six megabytes in 2025, and asks how much of that weight actually serves the visitor.

exhibits.title: Energy & e-waste
exhibits.hook: The cloud has a carbon bill, and the phone in your pocket has a landfill date.
exhibits.caption: Data centres, devices and the race to build new chips all consume energy and create electronic waste. As computing grows, so does the question of how to power and dispose of it.

exhibits.title: Quantum futures
exhibits.hook: What a working quantum computer might one day do, imagined from today's labs.
exhibits.caption: Quantum futures looks ahead at what fully scaled quantum computers might one day do, from simulating molecules to searching huge spaces. The milestones and their dates are speculative, not settled.
exhibits.caveat: Quantum futures describes ideas, not products; capability and timing are speculative.
exhibits.narration: Quantum futures looks ahead at what fully scaled quantum computers might one day do, from simulating molecules to searching huge spaces. The milestones and their dates are speculative, not settled.
